questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to explore the american culture and way of life. Having been there a couple times already, I wanted to go somewhere "authentic". Not many tourists venture to Montana, and I thought it'd be a great opportunity to experience the "real" The States. I also wanted to go somewhere where I could live a different life than the city life in Copenhagen, and I knew that Bozeman was a significantly smaller city surrounded by beautiful nature.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I loved living in Bozeman ! The only downsides were the expenses - rent in the States is super expensive - and not having my own room as I had to share my room with another student.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: MSU was very good at giving us all the information needed and gave us lists to follow to make sure we completed all the paperwork that was required.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I found the move in to be very easy and well organized. There were students and coordinators making sure that moving in to the dorms went as smooth as possible. There was also an orientation meeting and a bbq for the exchange students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Shared room and single room. As I wanted to save money and also wanted the "real" dorm experience, I chose the shared room.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: When you live on campus, you have to eat in the dining hall. You can either do the bronze plan and sort of your own food on the weekends, or pay a little more and eat in the dining hall on the weekends too.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I was lucky, as my roommate and I got along well. However, I did miss having my own room sometimes, as you're surrounded by people constantly (at least in my case, as my friends lived in the same dorm as I did), and sometimes need a break, where you can be completely alone. It is however quite expensive to get a single room, so you have to consider whether it's worth it. Other than that, living in the dorms was a very positive experience for me, as it was very convenient being able to walk to class, especially since I didn't have a car, and many of the off-campus housing options are far from campus, and biking almost isn't an option in winter with all the snowfall. Had I lived off campus, I also would've missed out on a lot of socializing among exchange students, as the majority of us lived in the same dorm (Johnstone). It was really nice living right next door to your friends and spending the majority of your time together, having all meals together, studying together. Living off campus might've have resulted in making more american friends however, so if you're looking to meet americans, perhaps living off campus is a better alternative, although there also were a few americans on our floor. As for the meal plan, I would recommend having the bronze plan, as the food in the dining halls on the weekends is supposedly lower quality, and also, you're probably going to be out exploring on the weekends anyways ;-)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As mentioned, housing is very expensive. Also, the kitchen facilities at least in my dorm were very poor.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I found registrering for classes really difficult, and spent A LOT of time and energy trying to figure it out.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I only figured out which courses were offered in the fall semester quite late, as I found the system to be very difficult to navigate. Many of the classes that I wanted to join were therefore already full, and I therefore ended up having to write quite a few professors asking them if I could join their class. As it was right before semester starts, some of the professors were too busy to respond and I therefore ended up having to go to some of their classes asking in person if I could join.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I used the MSU website to figure out what professor taught the courses and their emails, but sometimes it was difficult figuring out. The exchange student coordinator sometimes helped me establish contact with professors, when I couldn't figure out what professor to contact.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Luckily, many professors are inclined to let you in their class even though it's full, if you let them know that you're an exchange student. I was therefore in the end quite succesfull at registrering for the classes that I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to begin the registration as soon as it is possible, as many of the courses fill up quickly. Also, don't hesitate to reach out for help with your coordinator. I would also recommend registrering for more classes than you can take, as it is possible to drop classes the first week or so. In this way, you get to try the courses before having to commit to them.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: One of the courses that I did was a horticulture course, and I found this course to have a significantly lower level than the other courses I did. The remaining courses were in the environmental science department, and the level of the courses were quite high, equal to the level at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching in the States is similar to gymnasiet in Denmark, as the style of teaching relies on a lot of homework, tests and many smaller assignments. Likewise, the exams don't count for your whole grade as it does at UCPH, as assignments and participation in class also influences your grades.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Restoration Ecology
Landscape Pedology 
Elementary Japanese
Vegetable Production
Intermediate Yoga

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I loved Landscape Pedology! The level was very high, so I was very challenged and learnt a lot. The professor is awesome. We went on field trips every week and I really liked both seeing the surrounding landscape as well as having the hands-on experience with the theory we'd been taught in class.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The unexpected costs include VISA, which costs around 3.000kr in total, and flights which were around 6.000kr. I also travelled for about 5 weeks in total and ended up spending around 20.000kr.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: As mentioned, housing is very expensive, and food likewise. The quality and selection of the food in the dining hall was quite high and very varied though. Groceries in the States are much more expensive than they are in Denmark, so I imagine food expenses would've been around the same, if I'd lived off campus.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are so many clubs that you can join and the majority of them are free! Sports, art, political and cultural clubs, you name it. At the beginning of the semester (at least in the fall) they have the katapalooza, a kind of festival on campus where all the clubs and almost all other organisations in town are present and you can talk to them, hear what they're about, and sign up.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I joined the ultimate team which was a lot of fun and also an opportunity to make friends with a lot of americans ;-) Experiencing the American sports culture was also an experience, as I found it to be very different than the Danish sports culture. I would also recommend doing some of the acitivty courses. I did intermediate yoga twice a week and it was really good!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I recommend doing as much hiking as possible on the weekends, before the snow falls (around october) if you're into that kind of stuff. Otherwise, there's plenty of opportunity of doing mountain biking, climbing, there are plenty of all those outdoor activities surrounding Bozeman. If you're going in the spring semester, be sure to bring your skiing gear and get the season pass for the bridgers (the closest skiing area. the snow is the best, I've ever skied). Make sure to visit surrounding national parks such as glacier, the tetons, yellowstone. Go to the hotsprings (especially the Norris hotsprings are amazing)! Rent a car in the holidays (much cheaper, if you're over 25 yrs) and go on rd trips! Make sure to acquire a national parks pass, that way you have unlimited access to all national parks in the states for a year for about $80. Bring a tent and sleeping bag with you, that way you won't have to rent it and it's much cheaper than staying in motels in the summer. Make sure to go to Zion Nt Park in Utah and Glacier Nt Park in Montana, they're some of the most beautiful places I've ever seen!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it was very easy to adjust to the local culture, as the american is very similar to the Danish in many ways, and in that we're quite exposed to American culture in Europe. Americans are generally more outgoing than Danish people which can both prove to be a little overwhelming but also makes it a lot easier to meet people.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join a club. Say yes, if someone invites you to something :-)

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: People are way more religious than what is the norm in Denmark. Be careful about openly criticizing religion. Also, Montana is a republican state, so don't assume that everyone shares the same opinions as you do ;-) Furthermore, the alcohol policy is way stricter than it is in Europe. You can't get into bars if you're under 21, you can't drink alcohol in the streets, all the bars close at 2 am.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: My favourite part about the american culture is how easy it is to talk to people, as they're far more inclined to approach you than people are in Denmark. I also loved that everyone is so polite, holding the door for you, saying sorry and how are you and thank you whenever they get the chance. Make sure to do the same!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Getting around without a car is quite challenging, so be sure to either buy a car or make friends with americans who have a car. 

If you're looking to make money while abroad, it's very easy to get a job on campus and they're usually quite well payed (and taxes are way lower than they are in Denmark). 

Make sure to bring gear for hiking, and get a national parks pass (you can buy it in information centers in the majority of national parks)!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you're thinking about going on exchange, just be aware that it's A LOT of paperwork. I was quite taken aback by this, as nobody tells you how much work it is. Also, keep in mind that going on exchange is not the same as travelling, there will be weekends where you won't be able to go exploring, simply because you have too much studying to do (depending on what courses you're doing ofc, but generally in the states there's a lot of homework). So don't expect your exchange to be one long holiday, it's not always just fun. However, it is fun and rewarding the majority of the time, so I'd say it's totally worth it, and you'll learn more about yourself and your field than if you're just staying in Denmark.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Knowing about myself that I'm able to go to another country and study and thrive there. If I can do that, I can do a lot of things :-) And ofc seeing so much beautiful nature (the states really has it all!), and having gotten an understanding of how diverse, beautiful and conflicted a country the states is.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
The paperwork maybe was the greatest challenge haha. 
Living in the dorms also for me was a challenge, because I realised how important having my own space is for me. 
Not being able to leave campus whenever I wanted, as I did not have a car.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
